toolUseResult.originalFile:
---
name: integration-subprocess-segfault-flake
description: "Root cause + measured rates of intermittent 'signal: segmentation fault' from spawned subprocesses under -race on darwin: rawSyscall lacks //go:norace, so TSan runs in the fork child. Affects any fork-heavy package, often silently."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 540681cb-37a8-48d9-b289-533d545fbe66
  modified: 2026-08-05T10:02:55.225Z
---

Under `-race` on **darwin**, a Go test that forks can die with `signal: segmentation fault`
in the child before `exec`. **Not our bug — a Go toolchain issue.**

**Root cause.** Crash report (`~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/*.ips`) says
`crashed on child side of fork pre-exec`, SIGSEGV at `0x8`, single-threaded child. Symbolized:

```
exec.Cmd.CombinedOutput → Run → Start → os.StartProcess → os.startProcess
  → syscall.forkExec → syscall.forkAndExecInChild → syscall.rawSyscall
    → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)   ← SIGSEGV
```

`forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace` and justifies calling rawSyscall because "they are
assembly functions". **Was true on darwin until Go 1.26**, which turned `rawSyscall` from a
bodiless runtime/assembly declaration into a real Go function (`rawsyscalln` refactor) —
without adding the `//go:norace` that Linux's `RawSyscall` carries explicitly "to avoid race
instrumentation if RawSyscall is called after fork". Verified by diffing
`syscall/syscall_darwin.go` between go1.25.6 (no body) and go1.26.0+ (body).
Upstream: golang/go#49138, #50172, #50323.

**Measured rates** (2026-08-05, quiet Mac Studio, macOS 26.6, go1.26.4):

| Command | Crash rate |
|---|---|
| single package `-race` (`./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`) | 0 / 8 runs |
| `go test -tags=integration -race ./...` | 1 / 4 runs |

`./...` runs many race-instrumented package binaries concurrently, which is the amplifier.
An earlier "~1 in 3" estimate was a small-sample artifact — do not quote it.

**It is often SILENT.** A fork-child crash only fails the suite when it lands on a subprocess
call whose error is checked; best-effort paths swallow it. Proven: a crash report at
2026-08-04 21:50 belongs to a `./...` run that exited 0 with no "segmentation fault" text
anywhere. So this has plausibly been happening since the Go 1.26 bump (repo moved
2026-02-22, `b58ccebae`) while only rarely being *visible* — which is why nobody reported it.

**Not confined to the integration package.** A reproduction landed in
`cmd/entire/cli/strategy` (`TestReconcileDisconnected_ModifiedEntries`, `git commit` fork) —
that package has ~153 exec call sites. Any fork-heavy race-instrumented package is exposed.

**Mitigation in tree:** `-race` is off for `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test` on darwin
(`mise-tasks/test/ci/integration/shard`) — that package is ~272/294 subprocess-driven and the
spawned binary is built without `-race`, so `-race` there only ever instrumented the harness.
Packages like `strategy` keep `-race` (they have real in-process concurrency) and stay exposed
on darwin. CI is Linux, immune.

**Caveat when investigating:** `.ips` retention here is only ~4 days and `Retired/` is empty,
so absence of old crash reports proves nothing about the past.

Distinct from [[go-git-reconcile-flake]] (go-git "object not found", not a segfault).
See also [[git-stash-untracked-pitfall]].

The decisive experiment, the command that crashed 1 in 4 under 1.26.4:

```

run1..run5   exit=0   segv=0
```

## So the fix is a one-line pin bump, not my PR

**PR #1899 should be closed.** It permanently trades away real race coverage to work around a bug that a patch bump eliminates. The correct change is `1.26.4` → `1.26.5` in `mise.toml` and `go.mod`.

**Don't file the gist.** It's a duplicate of a fixed issue, and it contains a false claim — *"Present in go1.26.0 through go1.26.5"*. Affected range is 1.26.0–1.26.4.

**The "often silent" finding was a mispairing.** `pr2ci.log` last wrote at 21:33:47; that crash child launched at 21:50:18.40 — 17 minutes apart, different run. I never had a single demonstrated silent instance. That claim is in the PR body and the gist, and it's the load-bearing premise for "this has been happening since February" — so that inference goes too.

Two commands, before writing a bug report: `diff` the newer Go already installed, and search the tracker for the `.ips` annotation string — #79804's title is nearly verbatim. I went deep on mechanism and never checked whether the mechanism was already known and fixed.

gh pr create --title "build: bump Go to 1.26.5 to fix -race fork-child crashes on darwin" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What

Bumps the Go pin from 1.26.4 to **1.26.5** in `mise.toml` and `go.mod`. 1.26.5 is the current stable release, and it fixes a Go bug that made `go test -race` intermittently fail on darwin with `signal: segmentation fault` from a spawned subprocess.

## The bug it fixes

The child of `fork()` crashed **before it could exec**, so the target binary (`git`, or the built `entire` CLI) never ran and produced no output. No Go panic, no race report — a different test hit each run, indistinguishable from a real regression in whatever you were working on.

Go 1.26 turned darwin's `syscall.rawSyscall` from a bodiless runtime/assembly declaration into an ordinary Go function, without adding `//go:norace`. `syscall.forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace` and justified calling `rawSyscall` from the fork child on the grounds that *"they are assembly functions"* — true on darwin until 1.26. So under `-race` the child ran TSan instrumentation and faulted:

```
os/exec.(*Cmd).CombinedOutput → Run → Start → os.StartProcess → os.startProcess
  → syscall.forkExec → syscall.forkAndExecInChild → syscall.rawSyscall
    → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)   ← SIGSEGV at 0x8
```

macOS crash reports confirm it directly: `asi: ["crashed on child side of fork pre-exec"]`, `EXC_BAD_ACCESS`, single-threaded child.

Upstream: [golang/go#79804](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/79804), 1.26 backport [#79806](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/79806). 1.26.5 adds `//go:norace` to `rawSyscall`, `rawSyscall6`, `rawSyscall9` and the `errno`/`errnoX`/`errnoPtr` helpers, and corrects the stale comment. Verifiable without leaving your machine:

```bash
diff $(mise where go@1.26.4)/src/syscall/syscall_darwin.go \
     $(mise where go@1.26.5)/src/syscall/syscall_darwin.go
```

## Scope

Affected range is **go1.26.0 – 1.26.4**, so this repo was exposed from the 1.26 bump (`b58ccebae`, 2026-02-22) until now. **darwin only**: Linux's `RawSyscall` has carried `//go:norace` all along (with a comment naming this exact hazard), and the other libc-based platforms (aix, solaris) still declare their `raw*` helpers without Go bodies, so nothing there is instrumentable. CI runs `ubuntu-latest` and was never affected.

## Test plan

| | go1.26.4 | go1.26.5 |
|---|---|---|
| `go test -tags=integration -race -count=1 ./...` | **1 crash / 4 runs** | **0 crashes / 5 runs** |

- `mise run check` green on 1.26.5 — with the **unmodified** `-race ./...` `test:ci` command, i.e. exactly the command that was crashing.
- `mise run lint` clean (`lint:go` 0 issues, `lint:gomod` clean after `go mod tidy` — no `go.sum` change).
- Canary 59 + 4 tests pass.

## Supersedes #1899

#1899 disabled `-race` for the integration package on darwin as a workaround. This makes that unnecessary, and is strictly better: the workaround permanently gave up race coverage that the toolchain bump restores. I'll close #1899 in favor of this.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

content.text:
Confirmed — exactly as you describe. Both from the code and from the test:

```
[entire] Pushing 1 checkpoint ref(s) to origin...
[entire] Some checkpoint refs diverged; syncing 1 ref(s) individually... pushed 0 of 1
fatal: '…/does-not-exist.git' does not appear to be a git repository
```

## The mechanism

`batchPushRefs` issues **one** `git push <remote-name> <refspecs…>`. Because the target is the remote *name*, git fans out to every push URL inside that single process, and any URL failing makes the whole invocation exit non-zero. So:

- `queue.Remove(existing)` sits behind `if batchErr == nil` — a partial failure removes **nothing**, not even the refs that landed.
- The per-ref recovery can't rescue it either: `pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery` runs `git push <remote-name>` for one ref, which fans out again, so it still hits the broken URL. `pushed` stays empty (`pushed 0 of 1`), and `Remove(pushed)` early-returns on `len(refs) == 0`.

We have no way to isolate a single URL, and the queue has no per-destination state to record it with — entries are `{"ref": …}` only.

## Two consequences worth being explicit about

**The refs did land on the healthy URL.** The test asserts that: `CheckpointExistsOnRemote(bareA, checkpointID)` passes while the ref stays queued. So the queue retains refs that are already present on some remotes. That's safe — the retry is idempotent, the healthy URL just reports up-to-date — but it means **the queue never drains while any push URL is broken.** A permanently dead mirror gives you a permanently non-empty queue, retried on every push, visible only on stderr. That's the "degrades toward will-retry, never toward silent loss" property working as designed, with that as the price.

**One diagnosability wart I noticed re-reading the output:** the recovery message hardcodes `"Some checkpoint refs diverged; syncing …"` regardless of *why* the batch failed. Here the cause was an unreachable URL, and the user is told their refs diverged. Cosmetic, but actively misleading for exactly the multi-URL case — worth a small follow-up to phrase it by cause (or neutrally) since divergence and unreachability want different user actions. content.text:
That proposal has a problem I'd want to flag before building it — and checking it turned up a pre-existing bug.

## The read side is pinned to the *fetch* URL

`FetchCheckpointRef` → `checkpointFetchTarget` (`checkpoint_ref.go:44`) → `fetchURLAuthoritative`, which reads `git remote get-url origin` — i.e. **`url[0]`**, never a pushurl. So if refs are pushed to `pushurl[0]`:

- **no `pushurl` configured** → `pushurl[0] == url[0]`. Push and read agree. Fine.
- **`pushurl` configured** → we'd write to `pushurl[0]` and read from `url[0]`, two different repos. The checkpoints become unreadable from any other clone. It still works locally only because the local ref is retained after push — so the split stays invisible until someone clones or resumes elsewhere, which is exactly when checkpoints matter.

Picking `url[0]` instead doesn't rescue it: a `pushurl` usually exists *because* `url` isn't writable (fetch upstream, push fork), so we'd be pushing session data at a repo we have no write access to.

So neither single-URL choice derived from the remote is coherent. The only coherent single destination is one used for **both** directions — which is what `checkpoint_remote` already is (`PushURL` and `FetchURL` both resolve it). That means for the "I don't want checkpoints everywhere" need, there may be nothing to build: the mechanism exists, and it keeps the principle we settled on for branch — a single destination comes from explicit config, never inferred from topology. Now with a mechanical reason, not just a philosophical one.

## The pre-existing bug this exposes

Today, with any `pushurl` set, refs are pushed to the pushurl repos while reads fetch from `url[0]` — so **a second clone already cannot hydrate them.** Your proposal wouldn't cause that; it just wouldn't fix it. It's squarely in #1897's topic and currently untested. I'd add a test for it (clone from `url[0]`, assert the checkpoint is unreachable) so the gap is pinned rather than folklore.

## What I'd actually build for the queue problem

If the goal is "a broken mirror shouldn't wedge the queue forever", the fix is **per-destination queue entries** — `{ref, destination}` instead of `{ref}`, drained and removed per URL. That keeps fan-out (so mirror users keep working, and reads keep resolving), and a dead mirror retains only its own entries. Cost: a queue format change and N pushes instead of one fan-out push. The fast-forward-only impossibility we hit on the branch backend barely bites here, since per-checkpoint refs only diverge if a backfill or migration rewrote the same checkpoint ID.

So my recommendation: **keep fan-out, make the queue per-destination, and leave single-destination to `checkpoint_remote`.**

That said — if you still want refs to go to one URL only, I'll build it, but then the read side has to move with it or we're shipping a write-only store. Which way do you want it?

content.text:
Answer: **it depends on the failure mode**, and the difference matters for us.

| First URL fails with… | Later URLs | Exit | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ref rejection** (non-fast-forward) | ✅ still pushed | 1 | `push_with_options` returns error → `errs++` → loop continues |
| **transport failure** (unreachable, auth, no such repo) | ❌ **skipped entirely** | 128 | `die()` — process exits inside `transport_get`/connect, never returns to the loop |

Case 2 output shows it plainly — `reject.git` rejected, and `good2.git` still got `* [new branch]`:

```
To ../reject.git
 ! [rejected]        HEAD -> main (non-fast-forward)
To ../good2.git
 * [new branch]      HEAD -> main
exit=1
```

Case 1, unreachable first:
```
fatal: '../MISSING.git' does not appear to be a git repository
exit=128
good.git got the ref? NO
```

So the `errs++`-no-`break` loop in `builtin/push.c:438` only describes the *recoverable* path. `die()` on a transport failure never reaches the accumulator.

## Why this matters for #1897 and the queue design

My earlier test put the unreachable URL **second**, so the healthy one had already been pushed and I concluded "refs land on the reachable URL and stay queued". **That conclusion is order-dependent and I stated it too broadly.** With the dead mirror listed *first*:

- checkpoint refs reach **nothing** — not even the healthy URL;
- the queue correctly retains everything (so no loss);
- but every subsequent push also dies at URL 1, so a single dead mirror in first position **blocks checkpoint sync entirely**, indefinitely, while the user's own branch pushes fail too (exit 128 is hard to miss, at least).

It also sharpens the per-destination-queue idea I recommended: pushing per URL rather than relying on fan-out would make a dead first mirror stop blocking the others — which is an argument *for* that design beyond just queue bookkeeping.

I'd add a second unreachable-URL test to #1897 with the bad URL **first**, asserting nothing reaches the healthy URL — that's the worse case and it's currently undocumented. Want me to add it, and fix the doc comment on the existing test to say the position was deliberate?

**My "write-only store" worry was overstated.** Walking it through properly: on the same machine the local ref still exists, so no fetch happens and read routing is irrelevant. A clone of `pushurl[0]` has that repo as *its* `url[0]`, so reads resolve there correctly. A clone of some other mirror finds nothing — but that's true today too. So the model is coherent and needs no read-side change: **checkpoints live in exactly one repo; clone that repo and reads work.**

One thing your inference doesn't cover, worth stating since it's the real trade: a *rejecting* first URL (non-fast-forward) does **not** block the others today, so under fan-out refs still reach mirrors 2..N. First-URL-only gives that up. Equivalent for the transport case, strictly less resilient for the rejection case, in exchange for a single deterministic destination. 12	
13	// refsPushDestination is where checkpoint refs are pushed, plus how to name that
14	// place in user-facing output.
15	type refsPushDestination struct {
16		// target is passed to git push / the recovery fetch: a remote name, or a URL.
17		target string
18		// display names the destination in progress and warning output.
19		display string
20		// checkpointRemote is true when target came from a configured
21		// checkpoint_remote, which gates the "a checkpoint remote is configured"
22		// hint — that hint must not fire for a URL we picked ourselves.
23		checkpointRemote bool
24		// ignoredPushURLs counts push URLs of a multi-URL remote that will NOT
25		// receive checkpoint refs. Zero in every single-destination topology.
26		ignoredPushURLs int
27	}
28	
29	// resolveRefsPushDestination picks the single destination for checkpoint-ref
30	// pushes.
31	//
32	// Checkpoint refs need ONE deterministic destination, because the push-discovery
33	// queue records only a ref (`{"ref": …}`) with no per-destination state: a ref is
34	// removed from the queue once "the push" succeeds, so "the push" has to mean one
35	// place. Relying on git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs breaks that
36	// in both directions — a single failing URL fails the whole invocation and no ref
37	// unqueues even though some URLs took it, and an unreachable FIRST URL makes git
38	// die() before it reaches any later URL at all.
39	//
40	// So when a remote carries more than one push URL we target its first push URL
41	// directly (the one git itself would push to first) and ignore the rest. The
42	// recovery fetch in fetchAndRebaseRefCommon uses the same target, so — unlike the
43	// fan-out path, which reconciled the remote's FETCH url while pushing to its
44	// pushurls — the URL we reconcile is finally the URL we push to.
45	//
46	// Consequences, deliberately accepted:
47	//   - Checkpoint refs live in exactly one repository. Cloning that repository
48	//     resolves them (its url becomes the clone's fetch URL); cloning a different
49	//     mirror of the same code does not. Mirroring checkpoints to several
50	//     repositories is what checkpoint_remote is for.
51	//   - A first push URL that REJECTS a ref (non-fast-forward) no longer lets later
52	//     URLs receive it. git would have carried on to them; we stop. That is the
53	//     price of a deterministic destination, and it is the case the queue can
54	//     actually reason about.
55	//
56	// The git-branch backend deliberately keeps git's fan-out: its v1 branch is a
57	// single shared ref with no queue to keep coherent, and mirroring it to every
58	// push URL is behavior users configure their remotes for.
59	//
60	// A single push URL keeps the remote NAME as the target rather than resolving it
61	// to a URL, so the overwhelmingly common topology behaves exactly as before —
62	// remote-tracking refs still update, output still says "origin", and no
63	// URL-keyed promisor config appears.
64	func resolveRefsPushDestination(ctx context.Context, ps pushSettings) refsPushDestination {
65		target := ps.pushTarget()
66	
67		// A configured checkpoint_remote is already a single explicit destination.
68		if ps.hasCheckpointURL() {
69			return refsPushDestination{target: target, display: displayPushTarget(target), checkpointRemote: true}
70		}
71	
72		// Pushing straight to a URL (git passes a bare URL through to the hook) is
73		// likewise already single-destination.
74		if remote.IsURL(target) {
75			return refsPushDestination{target: target, display: displayPushTarget(target)}
76		}
77	
78		urls, err := remote.GetPushURLs(ctx, target)
79		if err != nil {
80			// Not a configured remote, or git could not report its URLs. Keep the
81			// target as given; the push itself will report any real problem.
82			logging.Debug(ctx, "git-refs push: could not enumerate push URLs; using target as given",
83				slog.String("target", target),
84				slog.String("error", err.Error()),
85			)
86			return refsPushDestination{target: target, display: target}
87		}
88		if len(urls) < 2 {
89			return refsPushDestination{target: target, display: target}
90		}
91	
92		return refsPushDestination{
93			target:          urls[0],
94			display:         fmt.Sprintf("%s (first of %d push URLs)", remote.RedactURL(urls[0]), len(urls)),
95			ignoredPushURLs: len(urls) - 1,
96		}
97	}
98	
99	// warnIgnoredPushURLs tells the user, once per push, that checkpoint refs are
100	// going to one URL of a multi-URL remote — otherwise the choice is invisible and
101	// looks like the other mirrors silently lost their checkpoints.
102	func (d refsPushDestination) warnIgnoredPushURLs(ctx context.Context, errOut io.Writer) {
103		if d.ignoredPushURLs == 0 {
104			return
105		}
106		fmt.Fprintf(errOut, "[entire] Checkpoints go to one repository: %s. %d other push URL(s) of this remote will not receive them.\n",
107			d.display, d.ignoredPushURLs)
108		fmt.Fprintln(errOut, "[entire] To store checkpoints in a specific repository instead, set checkpoint_remote in .entire/settings.json.")
109		logging.Info(ctx, "git-refs push: multi-URL remote, pushing checkpoint refs to the first push URL only",
110			slog.String("target", remote.RedactURL(d.target)),
111			slog.Int("ignored_push_urls", d.ignoredPushURLs),
112		)
113	}

feat(checkpoint): push checkpoint refs to one destination, and say where

The git-refs push-discovery queue records only a ref (`{"ref": …}`) with no
per-destination state, so "this ref is pushed" has to mean one place. Relying on
git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs cannot provide that:

- one failing URL fails the whole `git push` invocation, so no ref unqueues even
  though other URLs took it — a dead mirror wedges the queue indefinitely;
- and git's iteration is not even uniform. A ref REJECTION returns and git
  carries on to later URLs, but a transport failure (missing repo, auth, bad
  host) die()s — so an unreachable FIRST push URL means nothing is pushed
  anywhere, while the same mirror in last position is harmless. Position
  silently decided the outcome.

So when a remote carries more than one push URL, checkpoint refs now target its
first push URL directly and the rest are skipped. The recovery fetch uses the
same target, which also fixes a mismatch: fan-out reconciled the remote's FETCH
url while pushing to its pushurls, so with a pushurl set we reconciled a repo
nothing was pushed to.

A single push URL keeps the remote NAME as the target, so the overwhelmingly
common topology is byte-identical to before — remote-tracking refs still update,
output still says "origin", no URL-keyed promisor config appears.

The git-branch backend deliberately keeps git's fan-out: its v1 branch is a
single shared ref with no queue to keep coherent, and mirroring it to every push
URL is what users configure those remotes for. The two backends therefore differ
on multi-URL remotes; that is documented at the decision point rather than left
to be discovered.

Trade accepted: checkpoint refs live in exactly one repository, so cloning a
different mirror of the same code will not find them, and a rejecting first URL
no longer lets later URLs receive the refs. checkpoint_remote remains the way to
name a checkpoint repository explicitly.

Because that is invisible otherwise, it is now announced in three places:
pre-push warns on stderr naming the chosen URL and how many were skipped;
`entire enable` notes it; `entire doctor` reports it under "Checkpoint
destination: REVIEW". All three also cover the other ambiguous topology —
several remotes, where checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to while
resume/explain always read via origin. All are silent on an ordinary repo and
whenever checkpoint_remote already pins a destination.

- the batch-rejection retry claimed "Some checkpoint refs diverged" for every
  failure, including an unreachable destination — sending users after the wrong
  problem. It now says the push was rejected without asserting why.
- printCheckpointRemoteHint ("a checkpoint remote is configured in Entire
  settings") fired for any URL target and would now fire for a URL we picked
  ourselves. It is gated on an actual checkpoint_remote.

## Why refs need one destination

The push-discovery queue records only a ref — `{"ref": …}`, no per-destination state — so *"this ref is pushed"* has to mean one place. git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs can't provide that, in two distinct ways:

1. **One failing URL fails the whole invocation**, so no ref unqueues even though other URLs took it. A dead mirror wedges the queue indefinitely, retried on every push.
2. **git's iteration isn't uniform.** A ref *rejection* returns and git carries on to later URLs; a *transport* failure (missing repo, auth, bad host) `die()`s. Verified:

| First URL fails with… | Later URLs | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| non-fast-forward rejection | ✅ still pushed | 1 |
| unreachable / transport | ❌ **skipped entirely** | 128 |

So an unreachable mirror in *first* position meant nothing was pushed anywhere, while the same mirror last was harmless. Position silently decided the outcome.

## What changes

When a remote carries **more than one push URL**, checkpoint refs target its **first push URL** directly and the rest are skipped. The recovery fetch uses the same target, which also fixes a real mismatch: fan-out reconciled the remote's *fetch* url while pushing to its pushurls, so with a `pushurl` configured we were reconciling a repository nothing had been pushed to.

More than one push URL → target `pushurl[0]` directly, skip the rest. Exactly one → keep passing the remote **name**, so the common topology is byte-identical (tracking refs, output, no promisor config). Recovery uses the same target, which fixes the mismatch where fan-out reconciled the *fetch* url while pushing to the pushurls.

Your `die()` question turned out to be the strongest argument for this, and I put it in the PR as the core justification: git's behavior isn't even uniform. A **rejection** returns and git continues to later URLs (exit 1); a **transport failure** `die()`s and skips them (exit 128). So under fan-out an unreachable mirror in *first* position meant nothing was pushed anywhere, while the same mirror last was harmless — position silently decided the outcome. That's now explicit instead of emergent.

git-branch keeps fan-out, guarded by the sync test from #1897. The backends deliberately differ on multi-URL remotes; documented at the decision point.

## The two warnings

Both cover **multiple push URLs** *and* **multiple remotes** — you said "multiple remotes" and those are different shapes, so rather than guess I handled both. The multi-remote case is worth saying out loud independently: checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to, while `resume`/`explain` always read via `origin`, so checkpoints pushed elsewhere aren't found again.


`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

Third agent in, and it caught two divergences that are real bugs, not style:

git add -A && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
refactor: address simplify review of the refs push destination

Cleanups from a four-angle review (reuse, simplification, efficiency, altitude).
No intended behavior change except where noted.

Efficiency — the one that mattered:

- resolveRefsPushDestination (and its `git remote get-url --push --all` spawn)
  ran before flushCheckpointRefsQueue's early returns, so EVERY push on the
  git-refs default backend paid a fork/exec for a destination that goes unused
  when nothing is queued — and multi-URL users got the "checkpoints go to one
  repository" warning on no-op pushes. It now resolves after both early returns,
  inside the existing push_checkpoint_refs perf span. Behavior change, and the
  intended one: the warning no longer fires on a push with an empty queue.
- inspectRemoteTopology replaced `git remote` + one `get-url --push --all` per
  remote (N+1 spawns) with a single `git remote -v`, which already applies git's
  pushurl-replaces-url rule and lists push URLs in order. Also removes an
  inconsistency where remote listing ran in repoRoot while the URL lookups
  inherited process CWD.

Correctness of what we tell the user:

- inspectRemoteTopology treated a checkpoint_remote *present in settings* as a
  pinned destination and went silent. But PushURL only honors it when it
  resolves — owner mismatch, unparseable URL and non-derivable protocol all fall
  back — so doctor stayed quiet while pushes really did go first-URL-only. It now
  asks remote.PushURL per remote, the "ask the client, don't re-resolve" rule
  CLAUDE.md documents for CoreOrigin().
- It also reported the first *sorted* remote that fans out, so a repo with a
  fanning-out `backup` remote that only ever pushes to origin got warned about a
  rule that never applied to it. Ambiguity is now per remote, and each is named.
- The git-branch explanation described the git-refs failure behavior ("retries on
  the next push"). Corrected: those URLs are reported and left behind, and only
  the fetch URL is ever reconciled.
- refsPushDestination.display was set from displayPushTarget, which maps ANY URL
  to the literal words "checkpoint remote" — so a self-picked push URL claimed to
  be a checkpoint remote while the struct's own checkpointRemote said false.
  display is now a method that names a resolved URL by its redacted URL.

Reuse and simplification:

- "redact if URL-shaped, else pass the path through" existed in three copies
  (two added by the previous commit, one pre-existing in redactGitArgs). Now one
  gitremote.RedactURLOrPath, forwarded through the checkpoint/remote facade.
- refsPushDestination drops its `display` field (a method), and the resolver's
  five branches collapse to three.
- checkCheckpointDestination and printCheckpointDestinationNote were the same
  four-step body; one function takes the header. `indent` was speculative
  generality (one value at both call sites) and is gone, as is the third
  redundant ambiguity check.
- warnIgnoredPushURLs uses the package's injectable stderrWriter instead of an
  io.Writer parameter both call sites hardcoded.
- Dropped the `pushTarget := dest.target` alias.
- Test helpers: one setPushURLs(remote, urls...) primitive under all three
  push-URL helpers, with position as the parameter — AddUnreachableFirstPushURL
  was a verbatim copy of the Second variant with the slice order flipped. The
  three doctor subtests became a table.

Stale rationale the previous commit invalidated: both file headers still said the
CLI "has no per-URL control at all", true only for git-branch now. Both carve out
git-refs.

Also fixed while in the file: checkCodexHookTrust's doc comment has been detached
from its function since before this branch (it sat above checkClaudeCodeHookDrift);
moved down to the function it documents.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
